tener · venir · poner · salir · hacer · decir · traer · oír · caer
column2: tengo · vengo · pongo · salgo · hago · digo · traigo · oigo · caigo

column1: Verbs in -cer / -cir after a vowel: what happens in the yo form?
column2:
-zco
conocer → conozco · parecer → parezco
conducir → conduzco · traducir → traduzco · ofrecer → ofrezco

Exceptions: hacer → hago, decir → digo (and their compounds: deshago, contradigo). Cocer → cuezo, being a stem-changer instead.

column1: haber in the present: what is missing from the paradigm he/has/ha/hemos/habéis/han?
column2:
The impersonal form hay = 'there is / there are'.

Hay un problema. Hay tres libros. (invariable — never han for plurals in standard usage)

The paradigm above is the auxiliary: he hablado. Plain ha does not mean 'there is'.

column1:
When and why do you use the
Presente de indicativo?
column2:
• Current state or action — vivo en Bath. Spanish does not need the progressive here.
  • Habit — como a las dos.
  • General truth — el agua hierve a cien grados.
  • Near future — mañana voy a Madrid. Very common in speech.
  • Vivid narration of the past — en 1492 Colón llega a América.
  • Offers as questions — ¿te ayudo? = shall I help you?

Reserve estoy hablando for action genuinely in progress right now. Trabajo en un banco = I work in a bank; estoy trabajando = I'm working at this moment.

column1:
Tricks and tips for the
Presente de indicativo
column2:
• -er and -ir are the same verb except nosotros/vosotros (comemos/vivimos, coméis/vivís).
  • The boot: stem changes hit every person except nosotros/vosotros. Same shape in the present subjunctive and commands.
  • Stem changes are unpredictable from the infinitive — contar changes, montar doesn't. Learn per verb.
  • The yo form is the master key: it builds the whole present subjunctive and all commands.
  • Tener, venir, decir are doubly irregular — yo-go and stem-changing.
